char, wchar_t, WCHAR and more

04 - Unicode/6.1 - char, wchar_t, WCHAR and more.md

char Data Type

This data type usually takes 1 byte of storage and uses ASCII character set, In C language a character is declared using char data type and a pointer to char presumably takes 4 bytes if made on a 32 bit system.

char initial = 'A';
char *name = "Arnav"; // String literal

Strings are declared using character array

char name[6] = "arnav\0";

To get the the bytes used by a string use sizeof operator, it returns the bytes used by an array or struct.

[!info] The ISO C Standard define how many bytes should there be in a data type, but there is no specification about how many bits should there be in a byte.

Read more on [[ISO C Standard and C Specifications|C Specifications and ISO C Standard]]

Wide Characters

[[6 - Wide Characters (The implementation of Unicode)|Wide characters]] are a separate entity from [[#char Data Type]] and don’t interfere with each other, wide characters in context of windows can be of two types [[5 - Unicode|Unicode]] and Multi-Byte Character which is an implementation of [[4 - Double Byte Character Set|DBCS]]. As we know the disadvantages of DBCS it is always better to use Unicode in place of Multi-Byte Character

Wide character functions and implementation are present in the [[Important Windows Headers and DLL’s#WINNT.H Architecture & Unicode Foundation|WINNT.H Header file]] in windows or, if we see the C standard library they will be present in wchar.h or string.h headers.

[!recap]- Why Multi-Byte Character were bad? There were many reasons but including [[4 - Double Byte Character Set#^3ebee3|Trail Byte]] error and others but in case of windows If you choose Multi-Byte, your program will actually be slower and less efficient. Here is why:

Since Windows NT, the Windows Operating System kernel natively speaks only 16-bit Unicode. If you set your project to “Multi-Byte,” you force your code to compile using the “A” functions (like MessageBoxA).

When your English-only app calls MessageBoxA("Hello"), the Windows OS has to:

  1. Pause your program.
  2. Allocate new memory.
  3. Translate your 8-bit “Hello” into a 16-bit Wide Character L"Hello" (using the active Code Page).
  4. Pass that newly translated string to MessageBoxW.
  5. Free the temporary memory.

This process is called Thunking. By choosing “Use Unicode Character Set,” you skip the translation layer entirely. Your program speaks the kernel’s native language, resulting in a cleaner, faster, and more robust Win32 application.

[!important]- Your choice of implementation A software engineer must draw a strict line between internal logic and external communication. While relying on 8-bit Multi-Byte strings is detrimental at the operating system level, an application is not forced to use memory-heavy 16-bit Unicode for its own internal data. To conserve physical RAM, massive text datasets should be processed using highly efficient 8-bit formats. The problem of character encoding only materializes when data crosses the boundary to interact with the OS. Within its own memory space, the application remains sovereign.

Single Source

When writing program you may want to write the program in Unicode and in ASCII, but that means you need to maintain two different code sources to prevent that Microsoft had implemented a TCHAR.h this is like a rewritten version of stdio.h because that provide alias for function like

  • printf and wprintf to _tprintf
  • strcpy and wcscpy to _tcscpy

Internal implementation is as following

#ifdef UNICODE
#define _tcslen wcslen
#elif
#define _tcslen strlen
#endif
